classification: Editorial interpretation of retained outcomes; no new experiments or threshold estimation

replacements.before: A Reproducible Benchmark of Receipt Assisted Passive Feedback and Authenticated Routing in Wireless Sensor Networks
replacements.after: Failure Boundaries of Censored Passive Feedback in Authenticated Wireless Sensor Routing

replacements.before: Missing forwarding evidence can reflect packet loss, contention or an unobserved transmission, making feedback design a joint problem of inference and airtime. We benchmark ACK-gated censored passive feedback against active proofs in 750 IEEE 802.15.4 runs on 30 new fixtures, with naive-passive, frozen-prior and capacity-matched policy controls. Under blackholes, delivery increases from 71.28% to 75.94%, a paired gain of 4.67 percentage points (95% interval 2.36–6.97; Holm-adjusted p=0.0161). Energy per delivered byte falls while total modeled radio energy rises slightly. The controls do not establish a unique censoring or attention advantage. A separate 180-run experiment tests frozen policies over authenticated messages and node-local records. Attention delivers 81.61% in benign conditions and 61.11% under selective dropping, without an established advantage over greedy or multilayer-perceptron routing. In 600 Cooja transfer runs, a relay that starts dropping after warm-up exposes a failure: delivery with scheduled processing delays is 32.94% with censored feedback and 79.11% with active proofs. A further 240-run factorial study separates proof traffic from evidence handling; adding proofs reduces delivery by 6.11 percentage points with always-on listening. A fixed-point MCU actor reduces signed-receipt deadline misses; a separate source-authenticated receipt profile meets its tested deadlines while retaining deferred public signatures. An exploratory 60–300 s extension exposes routing-energy exhaustion and increasing service debt. The contribution is a traceable comparison of feedback mechanisms and transport boundaries; the evidence does not establish sustained operation, physical-board performance, measured energy consumption or absolute deadline compliance.
replacements.after: Censoring missing forwarding evidence avoids treating every unobserved transmission as malicious, but it also removes a route for revising earlier positive evidence. We benchmark this trade-off using active-proof, naive-passive, frozen-prior and capacity-matched routing controls. In 750 IEEE 802.15.4 runs on thirty new fixtures, ACK-gated censored feedback raises blackhole delivery from 71.28% to 75.94% relative to active proofs, a paired gain of 4.67 percentage points (95% interval 2.36–6.97; Holm-adjusted p=0.0161). This conditional gain does not establish a unique censoring or attention advantage. A separate 600-run Cooja transfer experiment exposes a failure after a previously cooperative relay begins dropping traffic: with scheduled processing delays, censored feedback delivers 32.94% and active proofs 79.11%. Enabling proof generation while retaining censored evidence delivers 32.83%, indicating that proof generation alone does not restore delivery in this setting. These experiments use different implementations and cannot isolate behavior change as the sole cause of their contrasting outcomes. Separate authenticated transfer and factorial studies retain the absence of demonstrated attention superiority and a proof-traffic penalty under always-on listening. Fixed-point MCU emulation improves execution, but signed-receipt deadline misses remain 68/200. The contribution is a reproducible characterization of conditional feedback performance and an exposed adaptation limitation, rather than a universally preferable routing mechanism. Fixed geometry, heuristic risk scores, scheduled processing delays and unmeasured physical RF and energy restrict deployment inference.

5.9 Cooja transfer and relay behavior change

replacements.before: The original 750-run benchmark supports replacing the tested active-proof mechanism within its prespecified margins. Because eligibility and expiry rules change together with control traffic, the observed difference cannot be assigned to proof airtime alone. Comparisons with naive passive and frozen prior do not establish a unique censoring effect after correction. Retaining the earlier unsuccessful architecture comparisons prevents the feedback result from being recast as evidence for neural-policy superiority.
replacements.after: The evidence supports a conditional feedback comparison. Censored feedback meets the original 750-run decision rule, yet loses substantially to active proofs in the separate delayed Cooja blackhole setting. These studies differ in topology, traffic, state construction and execution, so their contrast does not identify behavior change as the sole cause. Within Cooja, the censored-plus-proof control tests whether enabling proof generation under the retained censored rule restores delivery; it does not. Eligibility and expiry semantics still differ between active and censored arms, preventing attribution of the full gap to one update rule.

replacements.before: ACK-gated censored passive feedback improves blackhole delivery over active proofs by 4.67 percentage points in the prespecified thirty-fixture benchmark. Matched controls establish neither a unique censoring effect nor neural-policy superiority. The separate 180-run authenticated transfer study likewise shows no established attention advantage, while the 240-run factorial extension identifies a proof-traffic penalty under always-on listening. These findings apply to the declared feedback, traffic and radio models.
replacements.after: The benchmark identifies a conditional benefit and a consequential transfer failure. ACK-gated censored passive feedback improves blackhole delivery over active proofs by 4.67 percentage points in the original thirty-fixture study, but delivers 32.94% against 79.11% for active proofs in the separate delayed Cooja behavior-change setting. Matched controls establish neither a unique censoring advantage nor neural-policy superiority. These outcomes delimit the tested mechanisms; they do not locate a universal switching threshold between passive and active feedback.

replacements.before: Behavior change exposes a different boundary. In the 600-run Cooja delayed condition, active proofs deliver 79.11%, censored feedback 32.94% and naive feedback 54.89%; censored feedback with proof generation enabled delivers 32.83%. Censoring alone cannot reduce earlier positive trust when later observations disappear. Fixed-point MCU execution and fast private receipts improve narrower execution paths, but the original 90 ms signed-receipt target remains unmet. Physical RF, measured energy, production key storage and deployment performance remain unvalidated.
replacements.after: Censored feedback with proof generation enabled delivers 32.83% in that Cooja condition, while naive feedback delivers 54.89%. Keeping effective failure counts fixed prevents missing observations alone from reversing prior positive evidence; other routing inputs can still alter actions. This mechanism-level limitation and the retained negative outcomes define the benchmarking contribution. Fixed-point MCU execution and fast private receipts improve narrower paths, but signed-receipt deadline misses remain 68/200 and the original 90 ms target is unmet. added_paragraphs: 6.2 Interpretation of the exposed failure boundary

With the rate-anomaly term disabled, censored feedback keeps the effective failure count β at 1 and never decreases the effective success count α. If no new accepted evidence arrives, these counts and their derived risk coordinates remain unchanged. Positive observations can increase α, but subsequent silence supplies no corrective count. This follows from Eqs. (3)–(5); it is a property of the declared estimator, not evidence that every learned routing action must remain fixed. Cache freshness, link estimates, geometry and service debt can still change the selected relay.

Table 11 and Fig. 12 expose the practical consequence in the tested four-node transfer setting. The delayed active-minus-censored delivery contrast is +46.17 percentage points (95% paired interval +36.89 to +54.50; Holm-adjusted p=0.00016). Adding proof generation to censored feedback changes delivery by −0.11 percentage points (95% paired interval −0.50 to +0.39; Holm-adjusted p=1). The second contrast supplies no evidence of recovery from proof generation alone; its nonsignificance is not a population-equivalence result. Active-proof semantics include different eligibility and expiry rules, so the contrast does not isolate the effect of negative updates.

The benchmark exposes a failure condition rather than estimating its onset. Attack onset, warm-up duration, channel quality, geometry and checkpoint are not swept independently. A universal change-point, a safe passive-feedback operating region and the cost-optimal moment to request a proof therefore remain unidentified. The current paper reports that boundary honestly; an adaptive probing policy would be a new mechanism requiring a separately frozen evaluation.
